summary.text: A crystal is a solid whose atoms, molecules or ions are arranged in a highly ordered pattern, a lattice that extends in all directions.
Most metals, rocks, ceramics and ice are polycrystals, many microscopic crystals fused together, while glass, wax and many plastics are amorphous, with no periodic structure.
A crystal is defined by its atomic arrangement rather than its outer shape, though flat faces with sharp angles often make one easy to spot.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Greek krustallos, meaning both 'ice' and 'rock crystal'

facts.label: Typical size in rocks
facts.value: Fraction of a millimetre to several centimetres

items.prompt: A shop sells 'lead crystal' wine glasses. Scientifically speaking, what are they?

options.label: True crystals built around lead atoms
Polycrystals of many fused lead grains
Glass whose atoms have no repeating order
Crystals only where the surface was cut

items.explain: Despite the name, lead crystal is a type of glass, an amorphous solid with no periodic order even microscopically.

items.prompt: A steel spoon looks smooth and shows no flat crystal faces. Inside, how are its atoms most likely organized?

options.label: As many tiny crystals fused together
As one single crystal throughout
With no pattern at all, like glass
In loose layers that slide freely

items.explain: Most metals are polycrystals: many microscopic crystals fused into one solid, each grain ordered inside.

items.prompt: As a crystal grows, why do flat faces end up covering its surface?

options.label: Surrounding liquid wears its corners away
Atoms stick more easily to rough spots, so flat ones spread
Flat surfaces pull in new atoms fastest
Pressure from nearby rock presses it flat

items.explain: New atoms attach easily to rougher, less stable parts of the surface, so the flat, stable surfaces grow larger until they cover the crystal.

items.prompt: A grain inside a rock has no flat faces at all. Could it still be a true crystal?

options.label: No, a crystal must show flat faces
No, unless it is over a centimetre wide
Only if it formed from a cooling liquid
Yes, if its atoms repeat in a regular pattern

items.explain: A crystal is defined by its microscopic atomic arrangement, not its shape; grains in a polycrystalline solid often lack well-formed faces.

items.prompt: Two identical melts cool down: one solidifies into a crystal, the other into a glass. Which one gives off latent heat of fusion as it sets?

options.label: Only the glass
Only the crystal
Both, in equal amounts
Neither of them

items.explain: Forming a crystal releases the latent heat of fusion, but forming a glass does not.

items.prompt: The word 'crystal' comes from an ancient Greek word that also meant what?

options.label: Glass
Salt
Ice
Light

items.explain: The Greek krustallos meant both 'ice' and 'rock crystal', from kruos, 'icy cold, frost'.
